subject: ela
intro: Information does not only come from words. Charts, graphs, photographs, maps, and timelines all carry information too. When you integrate information, you combine what the text says with what a visual shows to build a fuller, more complete understanding of a topic than either source gives alone.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The Great Migration was one of the largest movements of people in American history. Between roughly 1916 and 1970, about six million Black Americans left the rural South and moved to cities in the North, Midwest, and West. Many were escaping unfair laws, violence, and limited job opportunities. In the growing factories of cities like Chicago, Detroit, and New York, they hoped to find steady work and a better life. The migration changed American cities forever, shaping music, food, politics, and neighborhoods. It did not happen all at once. The pace of movement rose and fell depending on wars, the economy, and the demand for factory workers.

Imagine a line graph beside this passage titled "Black Population of Chicago, 1910 to 1970." The line rises slowly from 1910 to 1916, climbs sharply between 1916 and 1920, dips slightly in the 1930s, then rises steeply again from 1940 to 1970.

How does the line graph add to your understanding of the information in the passage?

steps: First identify what the passage tells you: millions of people moved north over several decades, and the pace rose and fell with wars and the economy.
Next, identify what the graph shows: actual population numbers for one city over time, including the exact periods when growth was fast or slow.
Combine the two. The passage explains WHY movement sped up or slowed; the graph SHOWS when those changes happened in Chicago.

The graph makes the abstract idea of 'rising and falling pace' concrete by showing the sharp climbs around 1916 to 1920 and 1940 to 1970, which match the wartime demand for workers the passage mentions.
solution.answer: The graph turns the passage's general statement that the pace 'rose and fell' into specific, visible evidence. It shows the sharp population jumps in Chicago between 1916 and 1920 and again from 1940 to 1970, which line up with the wartime factory demand the passage describes. Together, the text explains the reasons and the graph proves the timing and scale, giving a fuller picture than either alone.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Honeybees are essential to farming. As they fly from flower to flower collecting nectar, they carry pollen with them, allowing plants to produce fruits and seeds. This process, called pollination, supports about one third of the food crops people eat. In recent years, beekeepers have reported alarming losses in their hives. Scientists point to several causes working together: pesticides that harm bees, diseases spread by tiny mites, and the loss of wildflower habitat where bees feed. Protecting bees means addressing all of these problems at once, not just one of them.

Imagine a pie chart beside this passage titled "Reported Causes of Honeybee Colony Loss." The chart shows three slices: Pesticides 40 percent, Mites and Disease 35 percent, Habitat Loss 25 percent.

How do the passage and the pie chart work together to explain honeybee losses?

steps: Identify the passage's main point: several causes work together to harm bees, and all must be addressed.
Identify what the pie chart adds: it breaks the causes into measurable shares so you can compare how much each contributes.
Notice the chart confirms the passage's claim that no single cause is responsible, because no slice is even half.
Combine: the text names the causes and argues they act together; the chart shows the relative size of each one.
solution.answer: The passage names three causes of bee loss and argues they must all be addressed. The pie chart adds specific proportions, showing pesticides at 40 percent, mites and disease at 35 percent, and habitat loss at 25 percent. Because no single slice reaches even half, the chart supports the passage's point that the problem has multiple causes working together. The text explains the causes while the chart measures their relative importance.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Mount Vesuvius is a volcano in southern Italy. In the year 79 CE, it erupted violently and buried the Roman city of Pompeii under thick layers of ash and rock. For centuries the city lay hidden and forgotten. When archaeologists began carefully digging it out, they discovered streets, houses, shops, and even loaves of bread preserved by the ash. These remains gave historians a remarkable window into daily Roman life. Vesuvius is still considered active today, and scientists monitor it closely because many people live nearby.

Imagine a labeled map beside this passage. It shows the Bay of Naples, with Mount Vesuvius marked at the center, the buried city of Pompeii to the southeast, the city of Herculaneum to the west, and modern Naples to the northwest. A shaded circle shows the area covered by ash in 79 CE.

What can you learn from the map that the passage alone does not tell you?

steps: List what the passage tells you: Vesuvius erupted, buried Pompeii, and is still monitored because people live nearby.
Now look at what the map shows that the words do not: the exact locations of Vesuvius, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and modern Naples, plus how far the ash spread.
Notice the map reveals Pompeii was not the only place affected, since Herculaneum also sits within the shaded ash circle.
The map also shows how close modern Naples is, which helps explain why scientists still watch the volcano.
solution.answer: The map shows information the passage leaves out: the precise positions of Vesuvius, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and modern Naples, and the size of the area buried by ash. It reveals that Pompeii was not the only city affected and that modern Naples sits close by. This makes the passage's final point, that the volcano is still dangerous because people live nearby, much clearer and more convincing.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Recycling helps communities reduce waste, but not all materials are recycled at the same rate. Aluminum cans are valuable and easy to melt down, so they are recycled often. Glass and paper are also commonly recycled. Plastic, however, is more complicated. There are many different types of plastic, and some are difficult or expensive to process. As a result, a large share of plastic still ends up in landfills even when people place it in recycling bins. Experts say that reducing the amount of plastic we use in the first place may matter more than recycling it.

Imagine a bar graph beside this passage titled "U.S. Recycling Rate by Material." The bars show: Aluminum 50 percent, Paper 65 percent, Glass 33 percent, Plastic 9 percent.

How does the bar graph support the argument the author makes in the passage?

steps: Find the author's argument: plastic is harder to recycle than other materials, so reducing plastic use may matter more than recycling it.
Read the graph values and compare plastic to the other materials.
Notice plastic's bar, at 9 percent, is far lower than paper, aluminum, or glass.
Connect the evidence to the claim: the very low plastic bar gives numerical proof for the author's point.
solution.answer: The bar graph gives numerical proof for the author's argument. Plastic is recycled at only 9 percent, far below paper at 65 percent, aluminum at 50 percent, and glass at 33 percent. This large gap supports the author's claim that plastic is much harder to recycle and that reducing plastic use may matter more than recycling it. The passage explains why plastic is difficult, and the graph shows just how much that difficulty affects real recycling rates.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Sleep is not a waste of time. While you sleep, your brain sorts and stores memories from the day, and your body repairs muscles and tissues. Scientists recommend that children between the ages of 6 and 12 get between 9 and 12 hours of sleep each night. Yet many students get far less, staying up late with homework, screens, and activities. Studies have found that students who sleep enough tend to have better focus, stronger memory, and steadier moods than those who do not.

Imagine a two-line graph beside this passage titled "Average Test Scores by Hours of Sleep." One line shows reading scores and the other shows math scores. Both lines rise steadily as nightly sleep increases from 5 hours to 9 hours, then level off after 9 hours.

Using both the passage and the graph, explain the relationship between sleep and school performance.

steps: Identify the passage's claim: students who sleep enough tend to focus better and remember more.
Read the graph's pattern: both reading and math scores climb as sleep increases up to 9 hours, then flatten.
Notice the graph adds a measurable pattern to the passage's general statement.
Combine: the leveling off after 9 hours matches the passage's recommended range of 9 to 12 hours.
solution.answer: The passage states that students who get enough sleep tend to focus and remember better. The graph supports this by showing that both reading and math scores rise as sleep increases from 5 to 9 hours. The scores then level off after 9 hours, which fits the passage's recommendation of 9 to 12 hours per night. Together they show that more sleep improves performance up to a healthy point, after which extra sleep brings little added benefit.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The invention of the printing press in the 1400s changed the world. Before it, books were copied slowly by hand, making them rare and expensive. Johannes Gutenberg's press used movable metal letters that could be arranged, inked, and pressed onto paper quickly. Suddenly, books could be produced in large numbers. Ideas spread faster than ever before, literacy grew, and ordinary people gained access to knowledge once limited to the wealthy and the clergy.

Imagine a bar graph beside this passage titled "Estimated Books Produced in Europe by Century." The bars rise sharply: 1300s very low, 1400s slightly higher, 1500s much taller, 1600s the tallest.

How does the bar graph help you understand the impact of the printing press described in the passage?
items.hint: Compare the bar for the 1400s, when the press was invented, to the bars for the centuries that follow.

steps: The passage says the press let books be produced in large numbers and spread ideas quickly.
The graph shows book production climbing steeply in the 1500s and 1600s, right after the press appeared in the 1400s.
The rising bars give visible proof of the explosion in book production the passage describes.
solution.answer: The graph shows book production rising sharply in the 1500s and 1600s, just after the printing press appeared in the 1400s. This gives visible, measurable proof of the passage's claim that the press allowed books to be produced in large numbers and helped ideas spread. The text explains the cause and the graph shows the dramatic effect.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Wildfires are a natural part of many forests, but they have grown larger and more frequent in recent decades. Hotter, drier weather dries out trees and brush, turning them into fuel. Once a fire starts, strong winds can spread it rapidly across the landscape. Firefighters work to control these blazes, but very large fires can burn for weeks. Scientists link the rise in severe wildfires to a warming climate and to the buildup of dead vegetation in forests that were not allowed to burn naturally.

Imagine a line graph beside this passage titled "Acres Burned by Wildfires in the Western U.S., 1985 to 2020." The line is jagged but trends clearly upward, with the highest peaks appearing after 2010.

How do the passage and the line graph together explain the wildfire problem?
items.hint: The passage gives the reasons; the graph shows the trend over time.

steps: The passage explains why fires have grown worse: hotter, drier weather and buildup of dead vegetation.
The graph shows that the total acres burned has trended upward, with the biggest peaks after 2010.
Together, the text gives the causes and the graph shows the worsening pattern over 35 years.
solution.answer: The passage explains the causes of worsening wildfires, such as hotter and drier weather and a buildup of dead vegetation. The line graph supports this by showing that the acres burned in the Western U.S. have trended upward since 1985, with the highest peaks after 2010. The text gives the reasons while the graph provides the measurable trend, together showing both why and how much the problem has grown.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The human body is mostly water. Water carries nutrients to cells, removes waste, cushions joints, and helps control body temperature. People lose water all day through sweat, breathing, and other processes, so they must replace it by drinking and eating. When a person does not take in enough water, they can become dehydrated, leading to tiredness, headaches, and trouble concentrating. Doctors suggest paying attention to thirst and drinking more during hot weather or exercise.

Imagine a labeled diagram beside this passage showing a human body outline. Arrows point to different parts with percentages: brain 73 percent water, lungs 83 percent water, muscles 79 percent water, bones 31 percent water, blood 90 percent water.

What does the diagram add to the information in the passage?
items.hint: The passage says the body is 'mostly water.' The diagram shows exactly how much water is in each part.

steps: The passage states the body is mostly water and explains what water does.
The diagram adds specific numbers for how much water different body parts contain.
The diagram makes the general phrase 'mostly water' concrete and surprising, since even bones are 31 percent water.
solution.answer: The passage states the body is mostly water but does not say how much. The diagram adds specific figures, such as blood at 90 percent, lungs at 83 percent, and even bones at 31 percent water. This turns the general phrase 'mostly water' into precise, surprising detail and shows that water is found throughout the entire body, deepening the understanding the passage begins.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Electric cars are becoming more common as people look for ways to reduce pollution. Unlike gasoline cars, electric cars produce no exhaust from a tailpipe. They run on batteries that are charged from the electric grid. Supporters say electric cars can lower the harmful gases that contribute to climate change. Critics point out that the electricity used to charge them sometimes comes from power plants that burn coal or gas, so the benefit depends on how the electricity is made. Still, as more electricity comes from clean sources like wind and solar, electric cars are expected to become cleaner over time.

Imagine a bar graph beside this passage titled "Yearly Sales of Electric Cars, 2015 to 2023." Each bar is taller than the one before, with the bars from 2020 onward rising especially fast.

How does the bar graph relate to the passage's discussion of electric cars?
items.hint: The passage says electric cars are 'becoming more common.' What does the graph show about that?

steps: The passage opens by saying electric cars are becoming more common.
The graph shows yearly sales rising every year, with especially fast growth after 2020.
The graph provides measurable proof of the trend the passage states in words.
solution.answer: The passage states that electric cars are becoming more common, and the bar graph provides measurable proof. Sales rise every year from 2015 to 2023, with especially fast growth after 2020. The graph confirms and strengthens the passage's opening claim by showing the actual upward trend in numbers, while the passage explains the reasons people are buying them.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The Nile River was the lifeline of ancient Egypt. Each year the river flooded, leaving behind rich black soil along its banks. Farmers planted crops in this fertile soil, growing enough food to support a great civilization. The Nile also served as a highway, allowing boats to carry people and goods up and down the river. Because the desert surrounded them on both sides, the Egyptians depended almost entirely on the Nile for water, food, and travel. Their calendar, their farming, and even their religion were tied to the river's yearly rhythm.

Imagine a map beside this passage showing the Nile River flowing north through Egypt to the Mediterranean Sea. A narrow green strip of farmland runs along both banks of the river, while tan desert stretches far on either side. Ancient cities are marked as dots along the green strip.

Using both the passage and the map, explain why the Nile was so important to ancient Egypt.
items.hint: Notice where the green farmland and the cities are located on the map compared to the desert.

steps: The passage explains the Nile provided fertile soil, food, water, and a route for travel in a land surrounded by desert.
The map shows the green farmland and the cities clustered in a thin strip right along the river, with desert everywhere else.
Together they show the Egyptians had almost no choice but to live near the Nile.
solution.answer: The passage explains that the Nile gave ancient Egypt fertile soil, food, water, and a route for travel in a desert land. The map makes this vivid by showing the green farmland and the cities packed into a thin strip directly along the river, with empty desert stretching far on both sides. Together they reveal that the Egyptians depended on the Nile because it was the only source of life in an otherwise dry and hostile landscape.
